meta.titre: Forces as Vectors: Finding the Resultant, Acceleration and Equilibrium
meta.sous_theme: Resultant of forces, Newton's second law, equilibrium
tags: resultant of vector forces and equilibrium

source.epreuve_titre: GCE O/L Additional Mathematics past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: Three porters pull the same cart at a market in Bafia, each in a different direction. Will the cart move, and how fast? The answer depends on the single force that replaces the three, called the resultant. In Additional Mathematics such forces are written with vectors, and the examiner asks for the resultant, then the acceleration, then perhaps unknown constants when the particle stays at rest. The method is short and the same each time.

items: A vector can be written as $x\mathbf{i}+y\mathbf{j}$ and added component by component.
Pythagoras' theorem gives the length of the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle, and $\tan$ gives an angle from two sides.
A force is measured in newtons, a mass in kilograms.

sections.contenu_markdown:
### Forces written as vectors

A force in a plane is written $\mathbf{F}=(x\mathbf{i}+y\mathbf{j})$ N, where $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are unit vectors along the two perpendicular axes. The **resultant** is the single force with the same effect as all the forces together: add the $\mathbf{i}$ components, and add the $\mathbf{j}$ components separately.

$$
\mathbf{R}=\left(\sum x\right)\mathbf{i}+\left(\sum y\right)\mathbf{j} \tag{1}
$$

For $\mathbf{R}=X\mathbf{i}+Y\mathbf{j}$, the magnitude and direction are

$$
|\mathbf{R}|=\sqrt{X^{2}+Y^{2}},\qquad \tan\alpha=\left|\frac{Y}{X}\right| \tag{2}
$$

where $\alpha$ is the acute angle with the $\mathbf{i}$ direction. Look at the signs of $X$ and $Y$ to place the direction in the right quadrant.

### Newton's second law

The resultant force on a particle of mass $m$ kg gives it an acceleration $\mathbf{a}$ in the same direction:

$$
\mathbf{R}=m\mathbf{a}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathbf{a}=\frac{1}{m}\mathbf{R} \tag{3}
$$

Force is in newtons (N), mass in kilograms (kg) and acceleration in m s$^{-2}$.

### Equilibrium

A particle is **in equilibrium** when its acceleration is zero, so the resultant force is zero. The $\mathbf{i}$ components add to zero **and** the $\mathbf{j}$ components add to zero. This gives two equations, enough to find two unknown constants in the forces.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When forces such as $(a\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j})$ and $(4\mathbf{i}+b\mathbf{j})$ are said to balance.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Forces $(a\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j})$, $(4\mathbf{i}+b\mathbf{j})$ and $(-2\mathbf{i}-7\mathbf{j})$ in equilibrium give $a+4-2=0$, so $a=-2$, and $3+b-7=0$, so $b=4$. Check by adding all three: $0\mathbf{i}+0\mathbf{j}$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked for the angle the resultant makes with the $\mathbf{i}$ direction.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Compute $\alpha=\tan^{-1}\left|\dfrac{Y}{X}\right|$, then measure anticlockwise from $\mathbf{i}$: $X>0,Y>0$ gives $\alpha$; $X<0,Y>0$ gives $180^\circ-\alpha$; $X<0,Y<0$ gives $180^\circ+\alpha$; $X>0,Y<0$ gives $360^\circ-\alpha$. For $\mathbf{R}=-3\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j}$ the angle is $180^\circ-53.1^\circ=126.9^\circ$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When one of several balanced forces stops acting.
variantes.contenu_markdown: If forces are in equilibrium, the resultant of all but one is the **opposite** of that one. When it is removed, the resultant of the others is $-\mathbf{F}$, and the acceleration is $-\mathbf{F}/m$.

sections.enonce_markdown: Three forces $\mathbf{F}_1=(2\mathbf{i}+5\mathbf{j})$ N, $\mathbf{F}_2=(-6\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})$ N and $\mathbf{F}_3=(7\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j})$ N act on a particle of mass $3$ kg. Find (a) the resultant force, (b) its magnitude and the angle it makes with $\mathbf{i}$, (c) the acceleration of the particle and its magnitude.

etapes.justification: Components along the same direction are added separately from the others.
Same rule for the second direction.
Use Pythagoras on the two components, formula (2).
Both components are positive, so the angle is the acute angle itself.
Divide the resultant by the mass, formula (3).

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) $\mathbf{R}=(3\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j})$ N. (b) $|\mathbf{R}|=5$ N, at $53.1^\circ$ to $\mathbf{i}$. (c) $\mathbf{a}=\left(\mathbf{i}+\dfrac{4}{3}\mathbf{j}\right)$ m s$^{-2}$, of magnitude about $1.67$ m s$^{-2}$.

items.erreur_markdown: The resultant of forces of $3$ N and $4$ N is always $7$ N.
items.pourquoi_faux: Forces are vectors. Magnitudes add only when the forces act in the same direction.
items.correction_markdown: Add components, not magnitudes. Perpendicular forces of 3 N and 4 N give a resultant of $\sqrt{3^{2}+4^{2}}=5$ N.

items.erreur_markdown: Resultant $=(3\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j})$ N and mass $2$ kg, so the acceleration is $(3\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j})$ m s$^{-2}$.
items.pourquoi_faux: Newton's second law is $\mathbf{R}=m\mathbf{a}$. Leaving out the mass gives the force, not the acceleration.

items.erreur_markdown: For $\mathbf{R}=(-3\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j})$ N, stating the direction is $53.1^\circ$ from $\mathbf{i}$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The calculator gives only the acute angle. The $\mathbf{i}$ component is negative, so the resultant points up and to the left.

items.erreur_markdown: 'In equilibrium' means each force is zero.
items.pourquoi_faux: Only the **total** is zero. The individual forces can be large and cancel each other.
items.correction_markdown: Set the sum of the $\mathbf{i}$ components to $0$ and the sum of the $\mathbf{j}$ components to $0$.

items.erreur_markdown: Adding an $\mathbf{i}$ component to a $\mathbf{j}$ component: $(3+4)=7$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The two directions are perpendicular and cannot be merged into one number.

items.enonce_markdown: The forces $(5\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})$ N, $(-2\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j})$ N and $(-2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})$ N act on a particle. Find the resultant and its magnitude to 3 significant figures.

Two forces $(7\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j})$ N and $(-3\mathbf{i}+11\mathbf{j})$ N are the only forces acting on a particle of mass $4$ kg. Find its acceleration as a vector and its magnitude to 3 significant figures.
items.solution_markdown: $\mathbf{R}=(7-3)\mathbf{i}+(-3+11)\mathbf{j}=4\mathbf{i}+8\mathbf{j}$. Then $\mathbf{a}=\dfrac{1}{4}(4\mathbf{i}+8\mathbf{j})=(\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j})$ m s$^{-2}$ and $|\mathbf{a}|=\sqrt{1+4}=\sqrt{5}=\mathbf{2.24}$ m s$^{-2}$.

items.enonce_markdown: The forces $\mathbf{F}_1=(p\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j})$ N, $\mathbf{F}_2=(3\mathbf{i}+q\mathbf{j})$ N and $\mathbf{F}_3=(-4\mathbf{i}+5\mathbf{j})$ N keep a particle in equilibrium. (a) Find $p$ and $q$. (b) The force $\mathbf{F}_3$ is removed. The particle has mass $2$ kg. Find its acceleration and the magnitude of the acceleration to 3 significant figures.
items.solution_markdown: (a) $\mathbf{i}$: $p+3-4=0$, so $\mathbf{p=1}$. $\mathbf{j}$: $2+q+5=0$, so $\mathbf{q=-7}$. (b) The remaining forces are $(4\mathbf{i}-5\mathbf{j})$ N, which is $-\mathbf{F}_3$, as expected. So $\mathbf{a}=\dfrac{1}{2}(4\mathbf{i}-5\mathbf{j})=(2\mathbf{i}-2.5\mathbf{j})$ m s$^{-2}$, and $|\mathbf{a}|=\sqrt{4+6.25}=\sqrt{10.25}=\mathbf{3.20}$ m s$^{-2}$.

items_markdown: The resultant is found by adding the $\mathbf{i}$ components and the $\mathbf{j}$ components separately.
Magnitude: $\sqrt{X^{2}+Y^{2}}$. Direction: $\tan\alpha=\left|\dfrac{Y}{X}\right|$, then place the angle in the right quadrant.
Newton's second law: $\mathbf{R}=m\mathbf{a}$, so $\mathbf{a}=\dfrac{1}{m}\mathbf{R}$ in the direction of $\mathbf{R}$.
Equilibrium means the resultant is zero: both sets of components sum to zero, giving two equations.
When one balanced force is removed, the others have a resultant equal and opposite to it.
